bibl.title: Microplastics in freshwaters and drinking water: Critical review and assessment of data quality

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the quality of the published evidence on microplastic occurrence in freshwater and drinking water
span.quote: Accordingly, we assessed the quality of fifty studies researching microplastics in drinking water and in its major freshwater sources. This includes an assessment of microplastic occurrence data from river and lake water, groundwater, tap water and bottled drinking water. Studies of occurrence in wastewater were also reviewed.

span.label: how reliable are the fifty studies reporting microplastic concentrations in drinking water and its sources
span.quote: However, there have been questions regarding the quality of these occurrence studies since there are no standard sampling, extraction and identification methods for microplastics.

span.label: a nine-criterion scoring instrument applied to fifty studies, with the result that four of them score positive on every criterion
span.quote: Microplastics are frequently present in freshwaters and drinking water, and number concentrations spanned ten orders of magnitude (1 × 10−2 to 108 #/m3) across individual samples and water types. However, only four out of 50 studies received positive scores for all proposed quality criteria, implying there is a significant need to improve quality assurance of microplastic sampling and analysis in water samples.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Microplastics are frequently present in freshwaters and drinking water, and number concentrations spanned ten orders of magnitude (1 × 10−2 to 108 #/m3) across individual samples and water types. However, only four out of 50 studies received positive scores for all proposed quality criteria, implying there is a significant need to improve quality assurance of microplastic sampling and analysis in water samples.

span.label: microplastics reported in freshwater and drinking water at concentrations spanning ten orders of magnitude across samples and water types
span.quote: Microplastics are frequently present in freshwaters and drinking water, and number concentrations spanned ten orders of magnitude (1 × 10−2 to 108 #/m3) across individual samples and water types. However, only four out of 50 studies received positive scores for all proposed quality criteria, implying there is a significant need to improve quality assurance of microplastic sampling and analysis in water samples.

span.label: nine criteria scored 2 (reliable), 1 (reliable to a limited extent) or 0 (unreliable), summed into a Total Accumulated Score out of 18, with an acceptance rule that is a FLOOR rather than an average - no zero on any criterion
span.term: nine criteria scored 2 (reliable), 1 (reliable to a limited extent) or 0 (unreliable), summed into a Total Accumulated Score out of 18, with an acceptance rule that is a FLOOR rather than an average - no zero on any criterion
span.quote: For each criterion a value of 2 (reliable), 1 (reliable to a limited extent) or 0 (unreliable) is assigned. A ‘Total Accumulated Score’ (TAS) is calculated by adding scores for individual criteria (maximum 18 points) ( Tables 1, S2, S3). For data to be considered sufficiently reliable, a study should preferably have no ‘zero’ values for any of the individual scores

span.label: the dominant source of microplastics is fragmentation of larger plastics or product wear - and the RATE of that fragmentation under natural conditions is unknown, so the source term of any exposure model is unconstrained
span.quote: Further, microplastics in the environment are difficult to identify and standardized methods do not exist ( Mintenig et al., 2018). The dominant source of microplastics often is the fragmentation of larger plastics or product wear, however the rate of fragmentation under natural conditions is unknown

span.label: ONLY FOUR OF FIFTY STUDIES SCORE POSITIVE ON EVERY CRITERION - eight per cent of the literature this field's risk assessments would draw on
span.quote: Microplastics are frequently present in freshwaters and drinking water, and number concentrations spanned ten orders of magnitude (1 × 10−2 to 108 #/m3) across individual samples and water types. However, only four out of 50 studies received positive scores for all proposed quality criteria, implying there is a significant need to improve quality assurance of microplastic sampling and analysis in water samples.

span.label: THE DEFINITION HAS ONE END MISSING: microplastics are characterised as polymer particles <=5 mm, and a formal definition for the LOWER size boundary does not exist - only a convention that below 1 micrometre they are usually called nanoplastics
span.quote: Microplastics are generally characterised as water-insoluble, solid polymer particles that are ≤5 mm in size ( Bergmann et al., 2015). A formal definition for the lower size boundary does not exist, but particles below 1 μm are usually referred to as nanoplastics rather than microplastic

span.label: there are no standard sampling, extraction or identification methods, which is the authors' stated reason for questioning the occurrence studies in the first place
span.quote: However, there have been questions regarding the quality of these occurrence studies since there are no standard sampling, extraction and identification methods for microplastics.

span.label: the physical and chemical properties, composition and concentration of the particles all vary, so `microplastic` names a population rather than a substance
span.quote: One key challenge in assessing the risks of microplastics to humans and the environment relates to the variability of the physical and chemical properties, composition and concentration of the particles.

span.label: the risks are stated to be debated and largely unknown, in the same paragraph that notes microplastics are often detected
span.quote: Although microplastics are often detected in the environment, the risks they pose are debated and largely unknown.

span.label: reliability scoring from regulatory toxicology - Klimisch-style criteria for judging whether a study's data may be used in hazard and risk assessment - applied to microplastic occurrence studies
span.quote: Recently, Hermsen et al. proposed a weight-of-evidence scoring method for studies of microplastic ingestion by marine biota ( Hermsen et al., 2018). This method defined minimum quality criteria for various aspects of the analytical procedure, such as sampling, sample treatment, use of controls and polymer identification. It assigns a score for each aspect and provides a total reliability score for data reported in a study.

span.label: the acceptance rule is a FLOOR on the individual criteria - no zero anywhere - rather than a threshold on the summed score
span.note: eliminates: a study with one fatal methodological gap passing because its other eight criteria are strong · outcome: held
span.quote: For each criterion a value of 2 (reliable), 1 (reliable to a limited extent) or 0 (unreliable) is assigned. A ‘Total Accumulated Score’ (TAS) is calculated by adding scores for individual criteria (maximum 18 points) ( Tables 1, S2, S3). For data to be considered sufficiently reliable, a study should preferably have no ‘zero’ values for any of the individual scores

span.label: `reproducibility` is redefined for the analytical context and the everyday reading is refused in the same sentence
span.note: eliminates: a criterion being read as `another lab would get this number`, which the authors say natural variability makes impossible · outcome: held
span.quote: Reproducibility does not imply that another researcher would obtain the same result, which is due to the variability in conditions inherent to nature. Reproducibility in the context of analytical chemistry refers to minimizing the contribution of random or systematic error to the total observed variability.

A formal definition for the lower size boundary does not exist, but particles below 1 μm are usually referred to as nanoplastics rather than microplastic

span.label: quality criteria
span.quote: The method uses nine crucial criteria, which are detailed below. Criteria relate to those that are common in analytical chemistry, such as reproducibility of described methods, precision, accuracy and sensitivity, which together determine the robustness of an applied method.
